findings.title: Historical hook errors are promoted to an undated current warning
findings.what: The source count is explicitly historical, but null liveConfig selects warning severity and the present-tense title “Stop hooks are firing with errors.” No event date is propagated into provenance or wording, so old evidence can appear current without the required “as of <date>” qualification.
findings.fix: Derive the newest valid stop-hook event date and always attach provenance.asOf; when current configuration cannot confirm the hook remains active, use historical/as-of wording and info severity.
findings.acceptance: Given three old error events and liveConfig=null, the recommendation is info severity, its title or detail contains the newest event date as “as of YYYY-MM-DD,” provenance.asOf matches it, and no present-tense current-failure assertion is emitted.
findings.verifyNote: Adversarial re-read confirmed lines 21-26 call the count historical while lines 34-40 deliberately retain current warning wording for null configuration; lines 45-66 contain no asOf field.

findings.title: Suggested hook fix disables genuine failures
findings.what: The action and note say the hook should still block on real or genuine failures, but the supplied command `your-check.sh || true` converts every nonzero result to success. Copying it removes the very failure signal the recommendation says to retain.
findings.fix: Replace the unconditional success fallback with a concrete conditional that distinguishes the documented advisory outcome from genuine failure, or omit the snippet until that distinction can be expressed safely.
findings.acceptance: A test executes the proposed decision logic against success, advisory, and genuine-failure exit codes and proves that only the advisory case becomes success while a genuine failure remains nonzero.
findings.verifyNote: The second pass re-read the complete action, note, and snippet. The contradiction survives directly: lines 25 and 31 promise selective blocking, while line 37 unconditionally masks all nonzero exits.

findings.title: MCP server names enable command injection in generated fixes
findings.what: Server names originate in parsed MCP state and are inserted raw into shell command lines and a double-quoted echo. A name containing whitespace, semicolon, command substitution, quotes, or a leading option changes the copied command and can execute attacker-controlled shell syntax.
findings.fix: Validate names against the CLI's canonical server-name grammar and shell-quote every argument and diagnostic value; pass `--` before the name if the CLI supports it. Refuse to emit an executable snippet for an invalid name.
findings.acceptance: Tests with spaces, quotes, semicolons, `$()`, newlines, and leading dashes prove the generated snippet parses each accepted name as exactly one inert argument and rejects unsupported names without emitting executable shell.
findings.verifyNote: Adversarial re-read confirmed names flow from blocking/advisory records at lines 91-93 into buildReauthCommands and buildGateSnippet without validation or quoting; no comparison file was needed.

findings.title: Generated MCP authentication fix is not copy-paste-safe
findings.what: The recommendation labels raw `claude mcp auth ${name}` lines as copyable fixes, but ordinary shell-significant characters split or alter the server argument. The resulting command may authenticate the wrong server, fail, or execute unintended syntax.
findings.fix: Use a tested POSIX shell-quoting helper for each server argument, validate the supported name domain, and mark the fix validated only after hostile-name and round-trip argument tests pass.
findings.acceptance: For every supported server name, copying the emitted snippet passes exactly that name as one argv element; hostile or unsupported names produce no executable fix and a clear manual-action message.
findings.verifyNote: The second pass confirmed line 72 performs raw interpolation and lines 122-147 expose it as the recommendation fix. This is reproducible from the dispatched file alone.

findings.title: Overload detector turns a fuzzy time join into a certain repayment claim
findings.what: Token rows are associated to retry errors only by a symmetric ±90-second window, yet the title/detail state that re-retries re-pay the cached prefix and that each re-attempt re-reads it. The returned recommendation has no structured provenance identifying the error fields, token fields, window, or approximate inference, so unrelated in-window cache reads can support an overconfident savings claim.
findings.fix: Add structured provenance citing apiErrors status/retryAttempt/timestamp/sessionId and token entry timestamp/cacheReadTokens, explicitly label the join approximate, and soften the claim to estimated associated cache-read waste unless an exact request identifier is available.
findings.acceptance: The recommendation passes provenance validation; its observations identify both artifact field sets and the 90-second window, its inference states the association is approximate, and its user-facing wording does not claim exact repayment from timestamp proximity alone.
findings.verifyNote: Adversarial re-read confirmed lines 54-68 construct only a timestamp window, while lines 89-94 make categorical repayment claims and the returned object through line 104 contains no provenance.
